newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian UCB just cannot stop pleasing investors.
newsitem.headline: Belgian UCB just cannot stop pleasing investors.

text.p: Chemicals, drugs and films group UCB, a Belgian-based niche player which saw profits more than double in the last five years, is going from strength to strength, pleasing its markets and investors alike.
After an increase in ordinary pre-tax profits by 33 percent in 1996 to 5.6 billion francs, UCB announced after Tuesday's shareholders meeting that a similar increase was likely in 1997.
That news, together with an announcement that a share split was being considered, propelled the stock to record close of 111,850 Belgian francs, up 11,050.

Analysts welcomed the planned split, saying it would boost liquidity. The split is expected to take place in 18 months' time when all physical dividend coupons to the paper will have been used up and new ones will need to be printed.
"A 'normal' value for such shares would be 2,000 to 3,000 francs," analyst Georges Piron at bank BBL said, who forecast a 50-for-1 split.

He added the share did not have much more upward potential. "All the good news has been discounted by the market...I would definitely not buy it...it is not a matter of quality...UCB is an exceptionally good story."
He forecast 1997 earnings per share of 3,636 francs, rising to 4,363 francs in 1998. EPS after tax and before exceptionals stood at 3,032 francs in 1996.
Caroline Lauwers at bank Degroof said a 30-for-1 split would be adequate to attract the small investors and UCB employees the company is targeting with the share split.

She said the profit growth rate forecast by UCB for 1997 was above analysts' consensus of 20 percent, but the news would only boost the share by so much. "At a price/earnings ratio of 27 the share is expensive, the market average is about 20."
She said French share Sanofi was the only European share in the same sector with a P/E of 27.
UCB's strengths lay in focusing on a few major products and digesting development costs before product launches to maximise profits from the products. "It is a growth stock," she said.
The share has been a runaway hit. Two years ago it was at 26,825 francs, one year ago at 59,300.
One of its attractions was that it was the only pharmaceuticals stock on the Brussels bourse. There is also lingering take-over potential for the company, analysts said.
The risk in UCB's strategy was that the group could become too dependable on a single product, such as its current star, anti-allergy drug Zyrtec, she noted, rating the share a 'hold'.
Drugs are UCB's largest contributor to pre-tax profits.

A salesman at Generale Bank said he liked the stock because of the success the company was having with Zyrtec in the U.S. "It built up market share quickly." There was also the promise of approval of Zyrtec in Japan at the start of 1998.
"It is a well-led company," he noted.
UCB is not alone in planning a share split.

Chemicals group Solvay has announced a 10-for-1 split to make the share more accessible to a larger group of investors and to bring the price more into line with similar shares in Anglo-Saxon markets.
"We are lowering the threshold," spokesman Paul Muys said.
The share, which went ex-dividend on Wednesday, closed 350 francs lower at 23,125 francs after having traded close to its 1997 high on Tuesday.
